subtopic: FRED PROJECTS, NEW BRUNSWICK
FRED PROJECTS, NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext: Of the thirty-three projects carried out in the Province of New Brunswick under the FRED Agreement what will be the estimated final cost of each project, what will be the financial responsibility of the federal government and what will be the financial responsibility of the Government of the Province of New Brunswick in each instance?

speakeroldname: Mr. Russell C. Honey (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Forestry and Rural Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development
subtopic: FRED PROJECTS, NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
A project cannot be declared "carried out" or complete nor can its estimated cost be given (due to fiscal funding and changing circumstances) until the term of the FRED agreement (10 years) has almost run its course.
Under a FRED agreement, projects are recommended to the treasury boards of both the federal and provincial governments by the joint advisory board, which is composed of senior federal and provincial officials. This advisory board has no authority to fund or implement a project but no project can be considered by either Treasury Board unless it has been recommended by the advisory board.
Funding of a project is done on a yearly basis by both governments. A project may continue for the life of the FRED agreement (up to 10 years) or may remain dormant for some years until reactivated on recommendation of the board. Funds allocated during a fiscal year may be adjusted between or among projects under a program within an agreement by mutual agreement of the federal and provincial FRED co-ordinators, but funds may not be moved from one program to another without FRED Board recommendation and approval by both treasury boards.

speechtext:
1.	Is the government giving any consideration to changing its approach to the growing problems of customs examination, collection and liability?

speakeroldname: Hon. Eric W. Kierans (Acting Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: CUSTOMS EXAMINATION, COLLECTION AND LIABILITY
speechtext:
1. Departmental officials continually assess changing trends in transportation and marketing practices to ensure that customs examination and release procedures are revised, consistent with the law, to facilitate expeditious delivery to the importer.
2. Recently established procedures include a pre-audit of entry documents by customs appraisers which, provided the officer is satisfied that adequate controls exist and that there is an accurate description of the shipment, permits delivery to be made without any undue delay. These procedures combined with a provision whereby the goods may be released under security posted by the importer or his agent allows for the delivery of imported goods prior to the payment of duty and tax. The present system is considered to approach, as nearly as possible under existing legislation, a straight line transaction.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, though I was absent from the house during debate on the second reading of this bill I followed with interest the representations made by some of my colleagues with regard to the discontinuance of rail passenger service in Newfoundland and I hope the sincerity and logic of their statements made some impression on the minister responsible.
It becomes increasingly obvious day by day that the people of Newfoundland were made the victims of a railroading-a con game between the provincial government of Newfoundland, which for the first time in its history has remained silent despite the pleas of the vast majority of the people, the municipalities, the labour organizations and
Canadian National Railways other responsible bodies whose right to the normal standard of transportation services will be affected, and the then minister of transport, the transplanted Newfoundlander who was imported into the province for reasons of political expediency to represent one of the districts. This is the man described in Richard Gwyn's book as the minister who devised and piloted through the Commons the epochal National Transportation Act of 1967, creating a $40,000 pullman class job for himself in the process. He is also described by the same author as speaking before a Burns' night audience in Newfoundland with tears in his eyes, crying "You will never know how much I owe you." Brother, how hypocritical can you get? I will tell him what he owes Newfoundlanders, Mr. Speaker: he owes them his conscience.
The only reason the transport commission gave for discontinuing passenger service was the fact that the service was losing $918,000 a year. I say that if the service is losing money it is because of the inefficiency of the management, it is not the fault of the passengers. Whom do you blame in any business, Mr. Speaker, for neglect and lack of efficiency? You blame the boss. And where is he now? The former president of the C.N.R. has a new job as chairman of BRINCO. BRINCO is the only hope Newfoundland has of ever becoming solvent. Yet they put a man in as head of this organization who failed even to operate the railway in Newfoundland at a break-even point, let alone make a profit.
If the Canadian National Railways could not operate the rail passenger service efficiently, how can anyone with any sense of business logic say that the same company can efficiently operate a bus service? Nobody in Newfoundland objects to the introduction of the bus service. Every province has the two sei vices. But when the C.N.R. has demonstrated its lack of efficiency as the operator of a ran passenger service, why take the gamble of going into the bus business to the tune of $950,000 for a start?
Are there not enough bus companies of proven efficiency, already operating at a profit, which are able to take on the franchise for Newfoundland? Are they not the logical ones to take the risk, when it is so obvious that the C.N.R. will most likely operate this venture too at a loss? Why should the people of Canada be taxed still further in this connection? Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask every member sitting in this House of Commons, representatives of the ten provinces of
November 13, 1968

Canadian National Railways Canada, regardless of political affiliation, whether they would stand for such blatant disregard of their constituents.
Perhaps I should tell them that a Canadian National Official in Moncton, headquarters of the company's Atlantic region, had this to say as reported in the Financial Post of June 22: Train travel is well established here . .. passenger revenues increased 63 per cent between 1962 and 1967, even though the red, white and blue plan reduced over-all fare levels. The number of train passengers has increased steadily.
If I were to tell hon. members that there is one town in my constitutency, the town of Howley, which does not even have a connecting road to the highway-the inhabitants would have to swim a mile if they ever wanted to get out in case of need-would they stand for these conditions? Is this justice, Mr. Speaker.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Would the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer), the Chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission, the premier of Newfoundland and the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson) take another trip from Port aux Basques to St. John's, as we six Newfoundland members did and which they refused to do, and talk to the employees of the Newfoundland railway, listen to the statements they make about the deterioration in the maintenance of the passenger service and listen to them tell of the deterioration in the condition of the trains that has been allowed to happen in order to uphold the camouflaged reasons the commission gives for discontinuance of the service? Why is the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo so silent? When his own constituents came out to greet the six federal members from Newfoundland on our arrival at Port aux Basques he was not there. Why did the largest demonstration take place in his constituency to support our cause in protesting the discontinuance of the rail passenger service while we were on our trip across Newfoundland on the Newfoundland Bullet?
Since royal commissions and task forces are the vogue now, why not create a task force to investigate the relevance of our arguments and assess the advisability of this action? Let them look at the terms of confederation and decide whether this action by two or three individuals is justified. Let them decide with a sense of humanity and justice whether this discriminatory act can better serve the people of Newfoundland. But, Mr. Speaker, let this utter disregard for human beings rest on the


conscience of those responsible in the years to come.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I wish to speak about the operation of the Canadian National Railways, particularly as it has affected the province of Newfoundland. During the year 1966, as has been said in this house before, the national railways even with padded accounts lost some $918,000 in Newfoundland and at the same time lost some $35,900,000 in their total operation in Canada. It seems strange to me that at that time the rail passenger service in Newfoundland was abolished without any consideration given to abolishment of the same rail passenger service in the rest of Canada. The reason given in the case of Newfoundland was that the rail passenger service was losing money. Well, the fact is that rail passenger service loses money in every province in Canada. If a principle is to be applied, it should be applied in the total Canadian context. One could imagine what would happen if the rail passenger service were abolished in the province of Quebec or in the province of Ontario. I do not think the federal government would be allowed to get away with that.
The C.N.R. should change its name to the C.M.R. It is no longer a national service; it is the Canadian mainland railway. Newfoundland has been placed on the system's expendable list. Newfoundland passengers have been downgraded below livestock, the service has been reduced and the public is expected to conform to the utility rather than the utility trying to meet the needs of the public. With the C.N.R.'s attitude in Newfoundland, as the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Peddle) mentioned, we have
39-	seat buses plus one lavatory. Knowing the C.N.R.'s philosophy as it applies to Newfoundland I expect they will probably be billed as
40-	passenger buses.
First of all, it is not a matter which involves only the people who travel from St. John's to Port aux Basques. People now using the rail passenger service come from the more isolated areas not near the trans-Canada highway. They come from places such as Bonavista and must travel some 75 to 80 miles in order to get to the trans-Canada highway. How are these people to be serviced in the winter? The roads are nearly impassable in the summer and certainly will be closed for most of the winter season. Must these people suffer and be unable to travel because of the decision of one man in the
November 13, 1968

transport commission? This man, Mr. Pick-ersgill, was very friendly to Newfoundland over the years. He and the premier of Newfoundland were known as the original wheeler-dealers for Newfoundland. While the premier of Newfoundland was popularly considered the wheel when spending money in Newfoundland, Mr. Pickersgill was an intricate part of the wheel, in fact the hub, and a self-greasing hub at that.
This man, Mr. Pickersgill, who owes Newfoundland so much is the same man who through his political acumen created in his own fashion a job at $40,000 a year. One could also say, regarding Mr. Pickersgill's attitude, that not only was he self-appointed to that job but that his attitude toward Newfoundland has been that of someone who has been self-anointed. In the years when Mr. Pickersgill and Mr. Smallwood were in their heyday we must realize just how the operation worked. We had the king of the pork barrel in Ottawa, the man who made the pork barrel work, dipping in and taking out the big slices of pork and slinging them down a very carnivorous gullet, Mr. Smallwood at the other end, who devoured it at the expense of the Newfoundland people. One could say that certain Newfoundlanders go fat from overeating. The great majority are now at the point of starvation because of the attitude of a few.
We have been renowned in Newfoundland during the past years for all kinds of deals. We have had tax deals, promotional deals and cost plus deals. This is the type of government we have had at the expense of the people of Newfoundland. We have poverty in Newfoundland that people in this house would find it difficult to conceive and now, to top it all off, we have the railway deal. If all the roads to the stations other than those on the trans-Canada highway were brought up to standard and paved, then possibly we would be getting something in return for the abandonment of the rail passenger service. But are we to have something taken away and replaced by something better? No. We are to have just another example of the federal government taking something away from the have-not provinces with no respect or consideration for regional disparity and no respect for human decency.
It is high time this government abandoned its bits and pieces approach to the affairs of Newfoundland and adopted a comprehensive, long range program aimed at bringing the tenth province fully into confederation. Basic
Canadian National Railways to any such co-ordinated plan is transportation. A modern and widespread transportation network is essential in creating and maintaining the diversified industry necessary for the economic rehabilitation of Newfoundland. An efficient and effective transportation system is essential to the development and expansion of Newfoundland's great basic industries of fishing and forestry. In the circumstances that exist, only the C.N.R. is available for the creation of such a transportation system. It is one of the many minor tragedies of modern Newfoundland that this national, publicly owned system is being forced to operate within the narrow confines of private business and thus being compelled inevitably to give profit priority over people.
Perhaps the greatest tragedy is the poverty of spirit and absence of imagination on the part of this government that permits a great instrument for national development to atrophy while Newfoundland's real need goes unnoticed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill, C-124, includes among other things provision for loans and other arrangements to assist Air Canada in meeting its obligations. This is the third reading stage of the bill. It is not automatic that we debate all third readings but because of a development of the last day or two I feel I should take a few minutes of the time of the house to say something with regard to the obligations of Air Canada. What I have in mind was previewed in the question that I put to the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Richardson) on orders of the day this afternoon, namely, the promise of the Liberal government, when Mr. Pearson was prime minister, to the people of Winnipeg that the maintenance and overhaul base would stay there at least until 1973.
As some hon. members are aware-certainly the people of Winnipeg are very much aware of it today-one of the members on the other side, the hon. member for Lachine (Mr. Rock), has been quoted as criticizing, in fact condemning, the Minister without Portfolio for his efforts to persuade the government of which he is a member to keep the base at Winnipeg. As I said, using a question as a means of saying it, I think the Minister without Portfolio should be commended rather than criticized for trying to persuade the government to keep its promise in this respect.
November 13, 1968

Canadian National Railways
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
As a matter oi fact, I want to say categorically that I believe the first thing which should be respected in this whole dispute or problem is the pledged word of the then prime minister of Canada. May I make it clear that the fact we have a different government and a different Prime Minister does not alter the situation. I point out that this is not just an assertion of mine. Indeed, when this matter was the subject of questioning on the floor of the house on Friday, November 1, the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Helly-er) referred to the commitment made by the previous prime minister to the people of Winnipeg and made it very clear that the commitment still stands.
Lest anyone thinks I am paraphrasing I should like to read a bit from page 2298 of Hansard for Friday, November 1. We were on the orders of the day and after three or four other questions had been asked, indeed seven or eight other questions, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) put this supplementary question:
Would the minister give an assurance to the people of Winnipeg, as well as to the employees in question, that the pledge given by right hon. Lester Pearson, then Prime Minister of Canada, is going to be carried out?
The response to that question by the Minister of Transport reads as follows:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. That commitment which was given by the former prime minister, and which was subsequently reiterated by me in Winnipeg, still stands.
It could not be stated any more clearly than that. I suggest that all of the arguments about the surveys and the reports of the experts have to take second place to the pledged word or there is just no way in which we can carry on. I might add to this that I find it pretty hard to take for the hon. member for Lachine and others to act as though Winnipeg is trying to take something away from Montreal, something that somehow or other belongs to Montreal. No one who looks at this objectively could swallow that line. This is a base that belongs to Winnipeg. Winnipeg is where Air Canada started in the old T.C.A. days. It is the retention of something that belongs to the people of Winnipeg which we feel we are seeking when we ask the government to see to it that the base stays there.
I recognize the right and responsibility of the management of Air Canada to look at these things in economic terms and decide


what is best in the pure economic sense, but when it comes to national policy such as placing industry round the country and coping with employment and unemployment in different areas, I submit that the government has a particular responsibility. If that responsibility involves a subsidy, and I question this despite all the reports that some people have made to this effect, it is up to the government to give it.
As I say, I am not going to take the time to go into all of the arguments back and forth on this issue. I just want to say that when we who come from Winnipeg, and I believe I am speaking for all members from Winnipeg- even if I am speaking for them I hope some of the others will get up and say it too-say we cannot accept the idea that we are trying to take something away from somebody else we do so because we are trying to do no such thing. We want something which we believe is ours and which the then prime minister of Canada said would stay at Winnipeg and would not be taken away from us.
I suppose my question to the Minister without Portfolio on orders of the day was a bit rhetorical. Perhaps it implied its own answer.
I would be grateful if he would take the opportunity in this debate on third reading, as I would be grateful if other members from Winnipeg would say a few words, of rising and saying that he agrees with me. I should be grateful if the hon. member for Winnipeg South, who happens to be that Minister without Portfolio, would take this opportunity. He deserves to be commended rather than criticized by a fellow Liberal member for taking the stand he has taken, namely, that the pledge or promise of the government of Canada should be maintained. I hope that Liberal members and other members of the house might take the same position.
I know we have had this issue before us in the house on occasions without number over the past several years. It goes back over the regimes of two or three governments. Normally, as I say, one would not raise this on the third reading of this kind of a bill, but it is of tremendous concern to the employees of Air Canada in my city and to all the people of Winnipeg that certain things are now being said, and I felt that the situation should be outlined in this more correct light.
I again offer my commendation to the hon. member for Winnipeg South for trying to persuade the government to maintain its pledge. Again I repeat that the first consideration which should be respected in this whole
November 13, 1968

matter is the pledged word of the government which are those words of the present Minister of Transport, spoken by the former prime minister and subsequently reiterated by him in Winnipeg. He said on Friday, November 1, that the commitment still stands. We insist that it be kept.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take the other side of the C.N.-A.C. credit card. Last week I asked the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Richardson) as the acting minister of transport whether the government has any intention of allowing carriers other than Air Canada to increase their service in and out of Edmonton to compensate for the loss in service resulting from Air Canada's winter schedule. The minister made it clear that these decisions were under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Transport Commission. He said they would be reviewed by that body.
Upon checking my facts again I asked the minister a few days ago if he would clarify the role of the commission regarding air line schedules. I make the point now that air line scheduling is the prerogative of the air line involved, not of the Canadian Transport Commission. However, the minister again told the house that the commission has responsibility for air line schedules and by this he implied that the commission has the authority to approve or disapprove of changes thereto. I am sure the minister did not deliberately mislead the house, but again I make the point that the air line decides on the amount of service given to a particular city, not the Canadian Transport Commission.
The minister said a few days ago that the commission will be reviewing Air Canada's winter schedule to Edmonton. As of this afternoon the commission had no such plans.
Air Canada is Canada's national air line. It is owned, financed and supported by the taxpayers of Canada. It reports to parliament through the Department of Transport, not through Mr. Pickersgill or his commission. If the minister is aware of facts that are not at my disposal I would appreciate it if he could clarify the role of the commission with regard to its involvement in air line schedule changes. It is my information that the commission does not have to approve such changes.
I should like to ask the minister whether he will in the near future make representations to the management of Air Canada to restore service in and out of Canada to its previous level. I need not point out that Edmonton is
Canadian National Railways the capital city of the province of Alberta and I have the honour to represent in this house a number of its citizens.
It appears to me that Edmonton is not going to get too far with Air Canada until we have some representation on the C.N.-A.C. board of directors. Since one of the members from southern Alberta has recently resigned from this board over the disagreement regarding the appointment of Mr. Seagrim, perhaps there may be some hope now for Edmonton representation. It is important that Alberta have proper representation, that appointments are not made as political rewards and that elderly persons are not added to this already ponderous board. We need some young blood to stimulate the old.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The treatment being accorded Edmonton by Air Canada is a disgrace. The Edmonton-Van-couver service has been reduced from 38 flights to 28 flights a week, and seating capacity from 4,200 to 2,900. Edmonton has only one direct dayline flight to Toronto. The Edmonton-Winnipeg service has been reduced from 42 flights a week in summer to 28 flights, and the seating capacity is down to 2,320 seats from 3,330. The government has shown no concern about protests from business, industry and the Alberta Aviation Council. The new winter schedule is a blow to the city of Edmonton and an insult by Air Canada and this government to the capital city of Alberta. If Air Canada cannot provide a reasonable service there is only one thing to do-let C.P.A. come in and do the run on a daily basis.
Again I say, Mr. Speaker, that we had the spectacle of the minister from Winnipeg hiding behind the coat-tails of the transportation commission and attempting to test the credulity of this house with the statement that the transport commission was responsible for setting the schedule. This is ridiculous. He knows as well as I do that the schedule is set by Air Canada, and he knows that Air Canada has cut back on the service to Edmonton residents deliberately and of its own volition. If people in Edmonton want to get any kind of service to the United States they are now forced to fly to Winnipeg first. Now we have the Minister without Portfolio making sure that Winnipeg is well taken care of, while Edmonton is being neglected. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer), who has the nominal responsibility in this regard, is so busy running round the country that he has no time to look after his own responsibilities
November 13, 1968

Canadian National Railways
The new winter schedule, which deprives Edmonton of service to which it is entitled on past performance, is causing harm to the city's economic expansion. At a time when air travel to and from Edmonton has been expanding at a rapid rate, Air Canada comes along and reduces the facilities. No reason has been given, because no reason can be given. I am asking the Minister without Portfolio and the Minister of Transport, when he returns, to put prejudice aside and reopen this question so that Edmonton will be given the service to which it is entitled. Failing that, the ministers can lend support to the granting of a daily flight plan to Canadian Pacific Airlines, who at least are willing to provide reasonable service if Air Canada is not.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in the debate on third reading of Bill C-124 I am very conscious of the fact that just a few days ago some of us spoke extensively on the resolution stage of the bill and asked a number of questions at the committee stage. I am very much aware of the fact that it is not usual, especially on a bill of this nature, to debate third reading. But the circumstances that prompt some of us to rise are also unusual. It is not every day that the government of this country condones a move on the part of two of its agencies, the Canadian Transport Commission and the C.N.R., to totally abandon rail passenger service in a whole province of this country. I submit that the circumstances are unusual, and consequently we feel obliged to make a few remarks on third reading of this bill.
I note again with regret, as have some of my colleagues, the absence from the house of the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Jamieson), the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. He has at no time indicated an interest in this subject save for a few remarks during the course of his speech in the debate on the Speech from the Throne. At that time he tried, in a very inadequate way, to defend the action of the C.N.R. and the Canadian Transport Commission, and in effect implied that the government of which he is a member was prepared to stand behind this unjust decision.
I wonder where the Minister of Defence Production, who sits in this house as the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, would be if tomorrow Canadian National Railways decided they were going to abolish the coastal service in Newfoundland. The Minister of Defence Production knows better than anybody in this

house what the consequences of such a move would be for the people it is his responsibility to represent here. The Newfoundland coastal service is absolutely essential to the people of the south coast of the province, whom the Minister of Defence Production represents in this house. Yet this is the next step in what we consider to be the total abandonment of Canadian National Railways services in the province of Newfoundland. We consider that the rail abandonment is merely the first step in a program of complete abandonment: first, the passenger service, second the coastal service and third the freight service. Then the C.N.R. transportation services will be gone completely.
We reiterate the point we made in the house two weeks ago, that until this becomes national policy, until it becomes the policy of the government of Canada to allow Canadian National Railways to abandon their train services in all the other provinces of Canada, we will oppose it. My submission, which is inherent in this whole question, relates to the entire concept of public transportation. Public transportation made this country what it is. I believe it is a well known fact that before any segment of the public transportation system of this country can be abandoned the people who depend on that particular segment must show, and show conclusively, that they no longer need the service and in fact that they no longer want it.
In my humble submission the opposite is true of Newfoundland. When the transport commission opened its hearings in St. John's, briefs were presented to the commission in opposition to the C.N.R. application. I know of no brief that was presented which supported the application of Canadian National Railways. Since that time petitions have been circulated throughout the province of Newfoundland. These petitions contain hundreds and hundreds of names of people from all walks of life. As a matter of fact, since we on this side of the house rose to speak a few days ago my colleagues and myself have received telegrams, letters and communications from every segment of Newfoundland's population including, I might add, most of the labour unions in that province. This is why I note with regret the fact that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and his colleagues failed to rise and support us in this house. At the present time an appeal has been lodged against the decision of the Canadian Transport Commission
November 13, 1968
allowing Canadian National Railways to abandon its train services. That appeal was initiated, I believe, by the Newfoundland Federation of Labour, with whom the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and his colleagues profess to have some sympathy.

Canadian National Railways
The point has been well made that in very few provinces of Canada where Canadian National Railways operates rail passenger services does it come anywhere near to operating in the black. As a matter of fact, I think it is fair to say most if not all of them, apart from some of the main interurban services, operate at a substantial loss.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this stage of our consideration of Bill No. C-124, you will allow me, I hope, to point out certain deficiencies in the administration of the C.N.R.
We all know that, originally, the C.N.R. took special pains to provide services in areas lacking in adequate transport facilities. Unfortunately, the closing down of several stations proves that the main reason for the founding of this company is being completely ignored. Stations are closed down in the interest of a greater centralization. I am not against the closing down of stations which have no reason for being kept open, but only against the unjustified disappearance of economically viable stations. In view of the fact that in the province of Quebec and in Newfoundland there are still important villages which have no paved road linking them with other parts of the country, in my opinion these stations should be most definitely maintained.
The C.N.R. services in those localities are not only essential but they could also make money, in my opinion, since there is practically no competition.
Mr. Speaker, it is important to re-examine carefully the centralization plans of the C.N.R. In my opinion, too much centralization can lead to the operating deficits that we know, to say nothing of the displacement of a number of workers who are the real victims.
I would like to mention here the fate of telegraph operators in particular. Several of those agents are called upon to do all types of work, except that for which they were trained. Those station agents are displaced

November 13, 1968

Canadian National Railways without their many years of service being taken into account. Stations are closed down without taking into account the accidents which can happen following the lack of traffic experts.
Men trained for the maintenance of tracks are dismissed, and those who are kept by the company are transferred to the maintenance of extended sections, sometimes twice as long as what they are humanly able to look after. The great number of accidents which occurred recently are the result of this new centralization policy. In fact, if one goes back to the past, damages caused by the derailment which happened in December 1966 at Riviere-a-Pierre, when 25 cars ran off the line, amounted to $1.5 million.
A train went off the track in the county of Kamouraska and following an investigation and an examination of certain important parts of the cars, we were informed that there were not enough maintenance men. In fact, trains do not stop long enough to be checked.
Two trains ran into one another in Drum-mondville, and the cause of this accident is still unknown. A few days later, in Ontario, two trains collided on the same track; the cause of the accident is unknown to date.
Mr. Speaker, air companies sometimes lose airplanes which crash on mountains or fall in the sea. When he learns of such a loss no member of the house, no citizen is surprised.
But when one learns that the Canadian National lost a train between Quebec and Montreal, for instance, one is entitled to wonder.
Mr. Speaker, I once was on a train which got lost between Montreal and Ottawa during the 1967 winter. This Canadian National train which was going to Ottawa, was switched on a C.P.R. track. It ran for eight miles before being traced. There were 250 people abroad, among whom were several members of the house. For the information of those who would doubt my word, I suggest that they inquire further about this of a former official of the Post Office Department, the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr), who was with us on that day. He will be able to tell you that we arrived in Ottawa forty-five minutes late.

I believe, as many others have said, that it should be clearly understood and emphasized, even repeated many times if necessary, that we are not taking anything away from Montreal or Quebec when we request the minister to give consideration to retaining the base in Winnipeg. Canadian National Railways
We are also conserned about the employees who have been with Air Canada since its inception. Mr. Speaker, I should like to voice briefly my objection to certain remarks made earlier by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) according to whom the Minister without Portfolio has been criticized by some of his colleagues in the Liberal party.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take but a few moments to outline to the house what I believe is a very shortsighted approach by the railways in connection with the relatively new potash industry in western Canada. By way of background, I want to inform the house as to the size of the industry at the moment and how large it is expected to become in years to come.
The potash industry, though relatively new, is rapidly overtaking the production of the entire world. The industry is centred in the province of Saskatchewan and has an adequate supply for something like 1,000 years. In other words, there is for the railways a potential market in the transport of potash. Although there are approximately only ten mines, by the year 1969 these will overtake Russia in production. By that year about 5.4 million tons of potash will be produced in Saskatchewan. Eight years from now world production will double from 16 million to 31 million tons. However, owing to overproduction in the last two years the industry is going through a very critical period. In the year 1971 the supply of potash will exceed the demand by 33 per cent.
Several factors have brought this situation about. As I have said, one is overproduction. In addition, new mines have been opened. There is a need, first of all, to educate countries on the use of fertilizers. Many countries lack the necessary resources. However, by 1977 supply and demand should level out.
I believe that the railway companies are, as it were, missing the boat in regard to transporting the products of this industry. As a result of the overproduction to which I have referred, mines have had to cut back on their production. They are operating at something like 20 per cent under capacity. Therefore
Canadian National Railways they are looking for economies, and one area they are exploring is that of transportation.
I might point out that it costs between $9 to $16 a ton to move the potash produced to the central markets of North America. It costs $9 a ton to transport it to Pacific ports, with an additional $29 a ton for ocean freight. However, these companies have been negotiating with United States railway companies, which have taken up the challenge that Canadian railway companies cannot seem to meet, and the Great Northern Railway has accepted the concept of unit train loading.
At the present time, I.M.C. mines at Ester-hazy are using trucks to transport their production of potash from the mine sites to Northgate in the United States where it is loaded on to United States unit trains for transportation to the Chicago-Minneapolis-St. Paul areas. It seems passing strange that railway companies operating in Canada, with rail beds laid and rolling stock available in an area of potential business for years to come, cannot see their way clear to transport the products of this industry, if not at a profit, at least at a rate sufficient to balance their books for the next few years until it does become profitable.
I do not see why any mining company should decide after a few years to revert to transporting its production by rail when it has been operating a fleet of trucks to move production to the United States border whence it is hauled by U.S. railway companies. Neither do I see why the U.S. railway companies should surrender the business, having operated their unit trains apparently at a profit. I understand that the potash industry is at present saving by this method something like $5 a ton, so surely there must have been room for a little leeway on the part of the railways.
I should like to refer to a very timely article that appeared in the Monetary Times for this month. Part of it reads as follows:
According to R. W. Puder, I.M.C. vice-president in charge of materials management at Skokie, 111., the decision to establish the truck operation was the direct result of the failure to negotiate satisfactory arrangements with Canadian railways which, he says, refuse to accept the unit train concept.
I have already indicated that Saskatchewan has 1,000 years' supply of potash. Apparently the trucking company transporting this potash is making a profit; otherwise I presume it would not do it. Also the U.S. railway companies must be making a profit or they would not be interested. Yet our own railway companies do not have the foresight to retain

Canadian National Railways this business for the next seven or eight years if necessary until world production equals world demand, at which time they could make a profit. The Canadian railway companies are quite prepared to cut down railway service in various parts of Canada, abandon railway lines in other places and raise freight rates, but they are not prepared to seek new business that obviously has tremendous potential. This leads me to suspect there has been some shortsighted and very short range thinking on the part of the railways. They have never indicated what the explanation is.

In addition, what is to happen to the railway town of Melville? It has always been a railway town. The employees will have to move and find other jobs because the train service is to be abandoned. Present services will be dislocated and the potential for growth will be curtailed. Why, Mr. Speaker? Because the railway companies do not wish to give the town any backing. They consider that in that area they have a captive market and they will not reduce freight rates from Churchill, even though the result may be that freight cars return empty. I said I would be brief, and I do not want to detain the house any longer. Railway revenues will drop. Every year the I.M.C. people will move out something like 1,200,000 tons, saving in the process $5 per ton. And this amount is to be moved at medium production levels. I believe the record should be kept straight. Air Canada, or Trans-Canada Air Lines as it was known for 30 or more years, had its headquarters, most of its departments, its planning staff and auditing staff located in the city of Winnipeg. I do not intend to put the whole sad story on the record step by step. But beginning in 1948 there were indications that the former Trans-Canada Air Lines was beginning to move departments from Winnipeg to Montreal.
In 1948 my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), asked the then minister of trade and commerce, Mr. C. D. Howe, for assurance that the headquarters and main departments of T.C.A. would not be moved from Winnipeg. He was given the most categorical assurance that this would not happen. These assurances were confirmed several months later by the then president of Trans-Canada Air Lines. From that date to today, however, there has been a gradual movement of Air Canada departments and personnel from Winnipeg to Montreal.
As I said on an earlier occasion and repeat today that decision to move, which must have been planned pretty carefully by the management of Air Canada, was never communicated to any minister of transport in the past 20 years until just a few years ago when the then president of Air Canada made a statement to the effect that the whole operation would terminate. When that happened there was, of course, consternation among the people of the city of Winnipeg. Representations were made by the widest group of organizations I have ever seen come together on any one question. These included the government of Manitoba, the city of Winnipeg, the muncipalities around Winnipeg, the chambers of commerce, the boards of trade, the trade unions and the farm organizations. They all made representations to the then government.
What happened at that time? The then prime minister, Mr. Pearson, made the categorical statement that the base would continue its operations at the city of Winnipeg at least until 1973. When the minister of transport, the present Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith), was in Winnipeg in 1963 he was asked whether the government had been given a firm guarantee that the base would continue its operations in Winnipeg until 1973. He said:
It is a firm fact that the base will be kept open for the next decade.

SUGGESTED TRANSFER OF AUTHORITY TO SECRETARY OF STATE AND EXPANSION OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of transferring the authority over the Historic Sites and Monuments Board to the Secretary of State and of expanding the responsibility of this board from concern for buildings and monuments of unique historical interest to general assistance in the preservation of towns, villages and landmarks of artistic, cultural or historical interest.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion is relatively simple and straightforward in both form and content. The first part of the motion suggests that the responsibility for the Historic Sites and Monuments Board should be transferred to the office of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier). The corollary of that transfer would be the transfer of the national historic sites service, which is in effect the civil service arm of that board. I think this would be a desirable phenomenon in any case. Its goals are really part of the general cultural policy which the government should be pursuing. Since the National Museum of Canada is now the responsibility of the Secretary of State, it would seem to make more sense to have the Historic Sites and Monuments Board in the same place.
I would, however, prefer to spend most of my time today speaking about the second part of the motion which suggests an expansion, in effect, of the terms of reference of the board. It is my suggestion that the board not be limited as it now is both in regard to funds and function. The terms of reference of the board are not sufficiently broad, and it could be doing a much more valuable job in relation to the preservation and encouragement of the maintenance of parts of our historic and cultural heritage.
My argument is that the present activities of the board are restricted by its initial concept and also perhaps by the approach of those who govern the board, which I believe
November 13, 1968

Historic Sites and Monuments Board is one of historical conservancy. It is interesting that the members of the board are almost, but not entirely, archivists or professors of history. There are on the board no architects, no urban planners, nobody concerned with the history of architecture, no landscape architects. Indeed, the orientation of the board and its origin I think can be clearly seen in a document provided to me by the Historic Sites and Monuments Board. This document indicates that in spite of the changes that have taken place since the board was established in 1919, the fundamental concept of the board has not changed. It is a federal body whose appointed members have the collective duty of advising the minister on what sites, events, persons, buildings and objects are of national historical importance. I emphasize the words "national historical importance."
The board's terms of reference are keyed to historical geography, since the Historic Sites and Monuments Act refers to "historic places." If one looks at the Historic Sites and Monuments Act one finds there are continual references to the historic aspect of the board's function. The minister may, by means of plaques or other signs or in any other suitable manner, mark or otherwise commemorate historic places. He may make agreements with any persons for marking or commemorating historic places and for the care and preservation of any places so marked or commemorated. The minister may establish historic museums. He can acquire, on behalf of Her Majesty in the right of Canada, any historic places or lands for historic museums. One sees that the emphasis is entirely on the historical aspect. If you look at the criteria which the board uses in assessing a project you see that such things are considered as:
The site or structure shall be closely associated or Identified with events that have shaped Canadian history in a prominent way-
Another criterion is:
The site or structure shall have been prominently associated with the life of a great Canadian or an important movement in Canadian history-
Another criterion is that the structure shall embody the distinguishing characteristics of an architectural type exceptionally valuable for the study of a style or method of construction or its period or be a noteable example of the work of an early master builder, designer or architect. An important consideration of the board in assessing projects is that the potential for illustrating Canadian history shall be high. In other words, there has been

what I would call an archival orientation, an emphasis upon the museum or historical function.
What have been the results of this policy? Since 1919 the Historic Sites and Monuments Board has noted 600 sites as being of national historic importance. It has established 31 major national historic parks, and it has preserved over 30 buildings-in almost 50 years of activity. I suggest this is certainly the result of insufficient funds but it is also a result of the restricted interpretation placed upon the words "national historic importance."
If we consider what other countries are doing in this regard we cannot but come to the conclusion that we are lagging behind. In the United Kingdom, for instance, the Historic Buildings Council is supporting 1,200 historic buildings at a cost of something like $20 million. The National Trust in Great Britain is responsible for 190 historic buildings and owns 400,000 acres of land. Indeed, the National Trust is, next to the government of Great Britain, the largest landowner in the country.
I would like to consider what the French are doing in this regard, because they have developed some very imaginative ideas in this area. They are supporting 10,000 classified monuments in France and have elaborated a whole system of financial assistance for the preservation of these monuments. The French government is prepared to provide 50 per cent of the total cost of renovating and maintaining historic monuments. It is supporting about 15,000 monuments and historic buildings listed in the supplementary inventory, and the state can meet up to 40 per cent of the cost of any repairs or maintenance considered necessary.
The French have a policy of encouraging by fiscal measures the owners of properties classified or listed as historic monuments by means of deducting from income tax a proportion of the expenses of repairing and maintaining these buildings. Very imaginatively they have developed a monthly television program called "Masterpieces in Peril" which informs the public not only of the dangers threatening certain monuments forming part of the national heritage but also of the efforts of voluntary rescue workers. They have also established a prize of $30,000 which is distributed each year to persons who have been instrumental in saving or working to save a monument.
Those are European examples and one might suggest that in France and England
November 13, 1968

there are more historic buildings and places of cultural interest which require to be preserved. But if you look at the United States, a country which we sometimes hear is lagging in cultural and spiritual matters, you find that since 1966 they have been spending over $10 million a year on projects designed to preserve the 17th, 18th and 19th century heritage of that country. Their earlier efforts which were limited, as we are now in Canada, to projects of national significance were found in 1966 to be unsatisfactory.
For instance, in respect of historic sites legislation in the United States it was said that earlier efforts to preserve historic sites had been limited for the most part to projects of national significance acquired and administered by the national trust with donated funds. On the state and local levels, where historic lands and buildings were increasingly endangered by the bulldozer, interest and activity in preservation varied widely. Because of this, in 1966 the Congress of the United States passed an act which was intended to foster interest in saving landmarks of both local and national significance. I emphasize, not simply national but also local significance.
As I have said, they are now spending something like $10 million a year on these projects. The Americans are doing some very imaginative things under their program in connection with the housing and urban development act. They conduct surveys of historic places; they prepare local and state plans for preservation programs; they plan specific preservation activities in urban renewal projects; they acquire, protect and enhance historic buildings and sites, as we do; they carry out special demonstration projects to develop and study significant preservation methods for the guidance of other communities.
This is one of the more interesting things they do. They acquire restorable buildings and resell them to private parties who agree to rehabilitate and maintain them according to the requirements of the urban renewal plan. These buildings are restored and refurbished, then sold to private parties who agree to rehabilitate and maintain them under the urban renewal plan.
In addition, the federal government of the United States makes grants available to assist in planning. For communities of under 50,000 population, the American government has even more extensive programs which are designed not simply to maintain buildings of unique or historic interest but buildings
Historic Sites and Monuments Board
worthy of preservation because of their beauty or interest.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
In the United States over 200 of these projects are now under way. It seems to me that in comparison with what other countries are doing the Canadian record of 30 buildings being supported by the Historic Sites and Monuments Board is really a pretty sorry accomplishment. We are lagging behind. I suspect that one of the reasons we are lagging behind is that the board, because of its terms of reference and the fact that it is now within the present department, is not sufficiently concerned with the preservation and maintenance of our cultural heritage. I do not see why the activities of this board should be limited to monuments of a national or historic significance. There are many buildings of local or regional interest which are well worthy of being preserved. I think we should be leading the provinces in this area and not simply following in their footsteps. It should be the federal government which should be concerned, much more that it has been, for instance, with the maintenance, preservation and restoration of the port area in Montreal. How many fine buildings have been lost by delay there? There are many areas in this country-the town of Niagara-on-the-Lake is one-where a great deal of help could be provided to maintain the legacy of our past.
It seems to me we should be investigating more actively the possibility of using tax credits for these purposes. We should be doing more to publicize the fine buildings we have. We should be doing more to encourage interest in them by tourists and travellers in Canada. I suggest that museums and institutions such as Upper Canada Village are fine, but I do not think we should adopt an archival approach to this problem.
We should try to maintain the tradition and the grace of some of the eighteenth and nineteenth century buildings which exist in this country. I think we should keep alive what was good in the past not simply because it is of unique or museum value but because it is good. The roots of heaven are to be found here on earth, but the roots of the present are to be found in the past. Many of the buildings in the Maritimes, Ontario and Quebec preserve a living tradition and living values which have gone into the make-up of what we are as Canadians today. I suggest we should preserve these buildings, and we should be more active in preserving them not simply for their historical significance but because they are part of the values which are

Historic Sites and Monuments Board embodied in the Canadian character. We should preserve them not simply because they are unique but because they are good and beautiful.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to support the hon. member who has introduced this motion. Like him I feel it is high time that parliament and the government gave more attention to the preservation of Canada's historic past. I am pleased that a member on the government side of the house has brought forward this motion at this time because there has not been too much enthusiasm from that quarter in supporting similar motions that we in this party have proposed from time to time in respect of this matter. The Historic Sites and Monuments Board has, as part of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, had a rather chequered career. I was responsible for it during the period when I was in charge of that department, and I was aware then that there had been serious neglect in bringing into focus the historic sites which are identified with Canada's pathway to nationhood.
I was fortunate to have the opportunity of being responsible for this board when we were planning our centennial year. As a result there was an upsurge of interest in the subject of preserving and perpetuating Canadian history, and plans went forward to have a major historic commemoration and restoration with the idea of perpetuating living examples of Canadian history in our historic sites. A major project in each province was contemplated. Of course the maritimes were emphasized because that is where a good deal of Canadian history had its beginning. It was during that period that plans went forward for Louisbourg. A project which will be completed shortly at Signal Hill was moved forward into the development stage. Plans were in progress for Citadel Hill in Halifax and right across the country even to the farthermost northern recesses of Canada in commemoration of Dawson City as a historic complex.
I find it interesting that the hon. member has broadened the concept in the resolution to include the preservation of towns, villages and landmarks of artistic, cultural or historical interest. I think the Dawson City complex was the first attempt on the part of Canada to commemorate a whole community which represented one of the high watermarks in the development of the Northwest Territories as it was known in those days. It has been

universally recognized through the poetry of Robert Service and the writings of Jack London and is one of the best known historic sites in any part of Canada.
Unfortunately the program that was started in preparation for the centennial has not been expanded beyond that point. I think we were perhaps sidetracked into other activities that became associated with our centennial celebrations. We concentrated on Expo, a major feature of our centennial which represented a huge investment, with the result that the program recommended by the advisory committee in the early planning stages of the centennial celebrations was sidetracked from the fundamental purpose of making 1967 a year when we would have major breakthroughs in the preservation and restoration of our historic past. Unfortunately, even the project for a national museum which would be of a standard befitting a country such as Canada was sidetracked for such projects as the national centre for the performing arts which has been under discussion in this house from time to time. The funds that could have been used for historic preservation and commemoration were drained off into these other projects.
I am hoping there will be general support for the hon. member's resolution because it puts back into proper focus the cultural and historic activity of our country which has been neglected far too long. Of course it also has other features. We often talk about the demands for spiritual and cultural pursuits in this age of growing leisure. When we think of that aspect of the modern society in Canada we immediately move into the whole area of the development not only of historic parks and monuments but also of recreational and national parks. Again this is an area in which the government has been moving very slowly or hardly at all in recent years.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
We have heard some talk in recent days that we will be moving forward to establish national parks in the days that lie ahead. However, there has been no change in this situation since 1963. It is not enough for the house to approve a resolution recommending that the functions of the Historic Sites and Monuments Board be transferred from the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to the department of the Secretary of State. This is an interesting change in the physical location of this particular function at the Ottawa level, but the problem is much more inclusive than that.
November 13, 19S8	COMMONS
I should like to suggest that not only Ottawa has responsibility in these matters. Our provinces are deeply involved in historic restoration and preservation. Indeed, many of the provinces have been much more active than Ottawa in this regard. Of course, some of the large urban centres have been active in preserving historic buildings within their borders. In so far as the provinces are concerned, I merely mention such major restorations and commemorations as the pioneer village and old Fort Henry in Ontario and Barkerville in British Columbia, which is a complete restoration of one of the gold rush cities along the gold rush trail. In Manitoba we have Fort Garry, and Lower Fort Garry is being developed as an animated historic site.
I have already mentioned Louisbourg, the largest project of this kind which is going forward in the province of Nova Scotia.
Although there is no mention of this in the resolution, I think it is only right to point out now that we might revitalize or even revive the federal-provincial parks committee which was set up back in the sixties in order to bring about a joint program under the auspices of Ottawa and the provincial governments so that Canada as a nation might move forward to do precisely what the hon. member has suggested this afternoon, to accelerate the program of preserving our historic sites.
There is one more subject that I feel should be mentioned at this time. If we are going to co-ordinate our museums, our historic sites and our historic parks program under the department of the Secretary of State for the sake of greater efficiency and, we trust, greater enthusiasm on the part of the government for its responsibilities in these matters, I think we might also give attention to bringing under the aegis of the Historic Sites and Monuments Board the activities of the National Battlefields Commission which operates as a separate entity in the province of Quebec. The sole responsibility of this commission is to preserve, protect and develop the battlefields in and around Quebec city which are associated with Canada's early history. It seems to me that there is absolutely no difference at all in the functions of the Historic Sites and Monuments Board and the activities of the National Battlefields Commission which has this one isolated and exclusive responsibility.
With these comments, Mr. Speaker, I support the resolution. This does not necessarily mean we are going to resolve the problem the hon. member has in mind. The mere shifting

Historic Sites and Monuments Board of this activity from one portfolio to another might mean a change, as I have indicated, in the physical location, but unless the government becomes more deeply involved in its responsibilities in this regard than it has since 1963, unless it revitalizes the program that was going forward in the early sixties, we are not going to achieve the results that I believe a great many members of this house would like to achieve. Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments about that notice of motion which deals with one of the most interesting problems for the Canadian people.
I reluctantly express an opinion contrary to that of my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Roberts). I am reluctant also because my position is the opposite to that of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) who was, before I had the honour of being a member of this house, Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, who is responsible for this matter relating to the Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
If we consider the problem according to a most current and logical theory, we will be inclined to say that it is logical, that the responsibility for the National Sites and Monuments Board rests with the Secretary of State.
We may appear at first sight to be considering only the cultural, social and intellectual aspect of this problem of development of historic sites, the preservation of historic buildings, and the classification of historic events
November 13, 1968

Historic Sites and Monuments Board during which prominent persons in our history became famous.
However, when a method gives good results, it is not logical to put it away and waste energy which we may need in other fields.
It is obvious that, according to our principles, we are in favour of change and development. However, we must consider that development so as to obtain the most immediate results. This is why I think the mover of this motion has forgotten the role which is now played by the Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada, not taking into consideration the environment in which it acts and the principles on which its recommendations are based.
I presume that the department, advised by the board, must also consider extensive projects as well as the available funds and the opportunities of finding specialized personnel in that field to carry out those projects.
For this reason, I am of the opinion that this board should remain under the department, as is the case at present. We should obviously, in keeping with the present policy of the government, tend towards improving government administration. But we can do that not by thinking immediately of making all sorts of changes but rather by stabilizing the structures we already have, in order to allow the board better to fulfil its terms of reference.
I think it is worthwhile to glance rapidly at the present status of this board and at the present policy of the government which actually has been in existence for many years. From what we know, the terms of reference of this board are very important indeed.
The Historic Sites and Monuments Board advises-and that is its main function-the minister responsible for the elaboration and implementation of a national development program with regard to historic sites on any subject of a historic nature.
It was said earlier, if I am not mistaken, that today the Board does not have enough architects, and engineers among its members.
I feel that at times several architects or engineers would be useful to the Board but since its responsibility is to advise the minister on national programs dealing with matters of a historic character and since it is made up of distinguished historians and of at least one archivist, those specialists can make appropriate and useful recommendations to the minister and then the architects, the engineers and the town planners can start implementing the program.

If we refer to our legislation, we can see that the National Parks Act gives the minister the responsibility I mentioned a few moments ago, that is the responsibility for the elaboration and implementation of a national development program with regard to historic sites or anything of a historic nature. The act gives that responsibility to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I cannot say or I cannot imagine why, at that time, the legislators did not give that responsibility to the Secretary of State, but I suppose that they then had serious reasons to give it to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
This responsibility was specified in 1953. When it was passed, the Historic Sites and Monuments Act provided the statutory base for the operation of the board and defined its role as an advisory one. This role is very well defined in section 5. In a booklet published by the National and Historic Parks Branch under the title "National Historic Sites Policy", we find this section 5 on page 2, which reads as follows:
The Board may receive and consider recommendations respecting the marking or commemoration of historic places, the establishment of historic museums and the administration, preservation and maintenance of historic places and historic museums, and shall advise the minister in carrying out his powers under this act.
It is fitting to recall that the board itself was established in 1919 and from that date until the act was passed in 1953, operated under order in council authority. It is interesting to see the results which the board achieved.
Since its establishment, more than 600 sites have been designated as being of national historic significance and 31 historic sites and parks of prime national interest have been opened to the public.
Furthermore, steps were taken to preserve more than 30 buildings designated as being of a national historic significance.
The board usually meets twice a year. That means that other bodies carry out the projects. At every meeting, the board reviews proposals or recommendations made by individuals or representatives of historical societies, provincial or municipal governments, organizations interested in historic persons, sites or events, to appraise the merits of every proposal according to its national rather than regional or local significance.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Research reports on subjects to be studied are prepared under the auspices of the research division of the Historic Sites Service
November 13, 1968

of Canada. The recommendations of the Board are then submitted to the ministers for their approval, in accordance with our legislation.
The Board is composed of fourteen members, twelve of whom represent the ten provinces. There are two representatives from Quebec, two from Ontario, and one for each of the eight other provinces. There is also the federal archivist and an official of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. The provincial representatives are appointed by ministerial decree and chosen on the basis of their ability as historians and archivists. Because the Board acts as an autonomous jury, it must take care to give the best possible advice. As the responsibilities of the Board have increased in the last few years, it has decided to establish special committees to increase the results of its research. Those committees dealt particularly with criteria for the selection of special subjects. It has established for example a committee which would particularly deal with fur-trading and primitive sites of Indian tribes.
With the passing years, the Board has felt necessary to determine a certain policy to help it to play its role. In March 1968, it tabled in the house a report on the policy of the historic national sites giving an outline of the criteria regulating the selection of those sites. It was, as it were, the synthesis of the policy adopted by the members of the Commission over the years, and it may be useful to mention again its achievements.
I think that I should stress the complexity of the work and of the present mandate not only of the Commission, which is not the only one to act in this field since it has but an advisory role, but also the related services which carry out these projects after planning them.
These are the criterions of the Commission and the various committees it sets up occasionally, and I quote:
It is a policy that national history sites shall be located within the geographical boundaries of Canada.
Secondly,
(i)	The site or structure shall be closely associated or identified with events that have shaped Canadian history in a prominent way, or illustrate effectively the broad cultural, social, political, economic or military patterns of Canadian history;
or
(ii)	The site or structure shall have been prominently associated with the life of a great Canadian personage;
2715
Historic Sites and Monuments Board or
(iii)	The site or structure shall have been prominently associated with an important movement in Canadian history;
or
(iv)	The site or structure shall shed light on or illustrate effectively the culture of a prehistoric people, or shall be associated with important archaeological discoveries which have affected ideas and concepts to a major degree;
or
(v)	The structure shall embody the distinguishing characteristics of an architectural type exceptionally valuable for the study of a styie or method of construction or its period or be a notable example of the work of an early master builder, designer or architect.
If the site or structure has religious importance, in order to be eligible it shall also be significant in other fields of Canadian history and shall be no longer in active use by a religious order or congregation.
The potential for illustrating Canadian history shall be high-that is the site or structure shall be such that it will be possible for the visitor to gain an understanding of the history with which it is associated.
The site shall possess integrity; that is, it shall be known to be what it is represented to be, and shall include the original site. A further important consideration would be the extent of original materials and workmanship remaining.
I am trying to prove that considering the carrying out of our projects, up to now, as well as the criteria which must be applied with regard to the terms of reference of the Board and to the service which must be provided, and in the light of the minister's responsibility-which was conferred upon him under the act-as well as of the co-operation which must exist among various organizations, not only the federal government, but also provincial and municipal authorities, before making drastic changes, the resulting costs should be borne in mind, at a time when the government is trying to balance its budget. When considering the co-operation among the experts and various agencies of the government, we bear in mind the costly duplication which would impede the progress and success of our projects.

I have suggested that departmental responsibility for this work be assigned to the Secretary of State. This seems logical, especially if one considers that the riding I represent is situated in the most southerly part of Ontario where so many great events in Canadian history have occurred but responsibility for preserving and commemorating the memory of the past lies with the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. To my mind, this is strange. If the change I am proposing can be made I feel it would be helpful in preserving and in some cases restoring all those things which belong to Canadians as a whole. The department of the Secretary of State has in the past been charged with maintaining and correlating records of everything we want to remember, and it is the logical place for the activities we are now considering.
These are a few short words only on a subject which is both interesting and vital. I hope that in some ways the objective in the mind of the mover of this motion can become an actuality. I attach great importance to this, believing that parts of our country with a special claim to fame should become, in a sense, the property of the people of Canada as a whole rather than just a section. The sponsor of the motion indicated that it was desired to maintain certain towns which at the moment are of regional interest. I feel that the idea could be broadened in its scope. Nevertheless I hope the motion succeeds in its objective, if not today then at some time in the future.
